facts.fact: Fiscal policy is the use of government revenue and expenditure to influence the economy, run by the Ministry of Finance, not the RBI.
Objectives of fiscal policy include growth, price stability, employment, balanced regional development and reducing income inequality.
Counter-cyclical fiscal policy raises expenditure and cuts taxes in a recession, moderating the business cycle.
Pro-cyclical fiscal policy raises spending and cuts taxes in a boom, amplifying fluctuations.
Expansionary policy (more spending, lower taxes) fights recession, e.g. PM Garib Kalyan Yojana during COVID-19; contractionary policy controls inflation.
Fiscal consolidation is the effort to reduce the fiscal deficit and public debt.
Reducing banks' SLR is a monetary tool of the RBI, not a method of deficit financing.
Deficit financing methods: borrowing from the RBI, market borrowing, external borrowing and printing currency.
Article 112 calls the Union Budget the Annual Financial Statement.
The Budget is prepared by the Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance.
In 2017 the Budget was advanced to 1 February, the Railway Budget was merged and the plan/non-plan classification was abolished.
Budget stages end with the Appropriation Bill followed by the Finance Bill.
Capital receipts create a liability or reduce assets — borrowings and disinvestment; interest received is a revenue receipt (UPSC 2025).
Acquisition of assets, loans from foreign governments and loans to States and UTs are all capital-budget items (UPSC 2016).
Defence, interest, salaries/pensions and subsidies were all non-plan expenditure (UPSC 2014).
Consolidated Fund needs Parliament's approval; Public Account (PF, small savings) does not; Contingency Fund is at the President's disposal.
Zero-Based Budgeting requires every expense to be justified afresh from a zero base.
Outcome budgeting tracks results of spending; gender budgeting applies a gender lens to allocations.
A balanced budget has revenue equal to expenditure; surplus and deficit budgets differ in sign.
DBT transfers subsidies directly into beneficiaries' bank accounts to curb leakages.
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − non-borrowed receipts = total borrowing requirement.
Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments.
Effective revenue deficit = revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets.
keys: grants for creation of capital assets

facts.fact: Monetised deficit is the part of the deficit financed by borrowing from the RBI.
The FRBM Act was enacted in August 2003 for inter-generational equity.
FRBM caps the Centre's fiscal deficit at 3% of GDP; States at 3% of GSDP.
FRBM's escape clause (Section 4(2)) allows breaches for national security, calamity, structural reform or sharp output fall.
The N.K. Singh Committee (2016) reviewed FRBM and recommended a debt anchor.
In a direct tax impact and incidence fall on the same person; indirect taxes are regressive.
Direct taxes are administered by the CBDT and indirect taxes by the CBIC.
Wealth Tax was abolished from 2016 and DDT from 2020.
The Laffer Curve (Arthur Laffer) relates tax rates to tax revenue — an inverted U.
Tax buoyancy = % change in tax revenue ÷ % change in GDP; elasticity excludes discretionary rate changes.
A Pigovian tax (A.C. Pigou) targets negative externalities such as carbon; a Tobin tax targets speculative currency trades.
A cess is earmarked for a specific purpose; a surcharge can be used for any purpose.
A higher tax-to-GDP ratio means less dependence on borrowing; a falling ratio indicates slowing growth (UPSC 2015).
Over the decade before 2017 neither the tax-GDP ratio nor the fiscal deficit rose steadily (UPSC 2017).
The Swaran Singh Committee proposed a duty to pay taxes as a Fundamental Duty, which was not adopted.
GST was introduced by the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act (2016) and rolled out on 1 July 2017.
GST is destination-based: CGST + SGST on intra-state sales, IGST by the Centre on inter-state sales.
The GST Council (Article 279A) is chaired by the Union Finance Minister; decisions need a three-fourths weighted majority.
In the GST Council the Centre has one-third and the States two-thirds of the votes; quorum is one-half.
Petroleum products, alcohol for human consumption and electricity are outside GST.
GST laws of 2017: CGST, IGST, UTGST and GST (Compensation to States) Acts.
GST 2.0 (effective 22 September 2025) has two main rates 5% and 18% plus a 40% sin/luxury rate; 12% and 28% were removed.
GST 2.0's estimated net revenue loss is about ₹48,000 crore.
Before GST 2.0 the slabs were 0, 5, 12, 18 and 28% (plus cess).
The Union Budget 2026-27 was presented on 1 February 2026 by Nirmala Sitharaman.
Union Budget 2026-27 targets a fiscal deficit of 4.3% of GDP.
Under the new regime no income tax is payable up to ₹12.75 lakh for the salaried (₹12 lakh + ₹75,000 standard deduction).
The Finance Commission is constituted by the President under Article 280.
The 15th Finance Commission recommended 41% vertical devolution to States.
The 16th Finance Commission (constituted 31 Dec 2023) is chaired by Arvind Panagariya and covers 2026-31.
The 14th Finance Commission (Y.V. Reddy) raised States' share from 32% to 42% (UPSC 2015).
AP's GSDP for 2026-27 is projected at ₹19,75,073 crore (~₹19.75 lakh crore), 12% growth.
AP 2026-27 expenditure (excluding debt repayment) is about ₹3.10 lakh crore and receipts excluding borrowings about ₹2.34 lakh crore.
AP 2026-27 fiscal deficit is 3.8% and revenue deficit 1.1% of GSDP.
AP own tax revenue 2026-27 is about ₹1.26 lakh crore, 6.4% of GSDP.
The AP FRBM Act, 2005 sets annual targets to cut AP's liabilities and deficits.
The State Finance Commission is constituted by the Governor under Articles 243-I and 243-Y.
The 16th FC recommends a fiscal-deficit limit of 3% of GSDP for States in 2026-31.
The 16th FC noted AP has the highest per-capita expenditure on social-security pensions.
AP's net borrowing for 2026-27 is about ₹75,168 crore.
Article 113 covers Demands for Grants (voted only by the Lok Sabha) and Article 114 the Appropriation Bill.
Article 115 provides for supplementary, additional and excess grants.
A vote on account is under Article 116, usually for two months (one-sixth of the estimate), and cannot change taxes.
An interim budget comes under Article 112 and can propose tax changes, unlike a vote on account.
Article 265: no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
Article 266 creates the Consolidated Fund and Public Account; Article 267 the Contingency Fund.
Under Article 293(3) a State that owes the Centre needs the Centre's consent to borrow (UPSC 2018).
Article 110 defines a Money Bill; the Rajya Sabha can delay it only 14 days.
Charged expenditure (President's emoluments, salaries of SC judges and CAG, debt charges) is not voted by Parliament.
Cut motions: policy cut reduces a demand to ₹1, economy cut by a specified amount, token cut by ₹100.
The guillotine puts all remaining demands to vote together on the last day.
The Contingency Fund of India Act is of 1950; the fund is held by the Finance Secretary; corpus ₹30,000 crore since 2021.
The first budget of British India was presented by James Wilson on 7 April 1860.
The first budget of independent India was presented by R.K. Shanmukham Chetty on 26 November 1947.
Morarji Desai presented the most Union Budgets (10).
Indira Gandhi was the first woman to present the Union Budget (1970).
The Railway Budget merger (2017) followed the Bibek Debroy Committee's advice.
Budget presentation time moved from 5 pm to 11 am in 2001.
Zero-Based Budgeting was developed by Peter Pyhrr and adopted in India in 1986.
India's Outcome Budget began in 2005 and Gender Budgeting in 2005-06; DBT began on 1 January 2013.
A State's budget (including AP's) is presented under Article 202.
Union Budget 2026-27 total expenditure is ₹53,47,315 crore and receipts other than borrowings ₹36,51,547 crore.
The 2025-26 revised fiscal deficit was 4.4% of GDP, meeting the below-4.5% goal.
Revenue deficit in 2026-27 is targeted at 1.5% of GDP.
Central outstanding liabilities are 55.6% of GDP in 2026-27, with a target of about 50% by March 2031.
Public capex was raised from ₹11.2 lakh crore to ₹12.2 lakh crore in 2026-27.
Interest is 26% of total expenditure and 40% of revenue receipts in 2026-27.
Budget 2026-27 left income-tax slabs unchanged.
Budget 2026-27 cut the MAT rate from 15% to 14%.
Budget 2026-27 raised STT on futures from 0.02% to 0.05% and on options from 0.1% to 0.15%.
TCS on education/medical remittances above ₹10 lakh was cut from 5% to 2%.
A tax holiday till 2047 was given to foreign firms offering cloud services from Indian data centres.
Biopharma SHAKTI gives ₹10,000 crore over five years for biologics and biosimilars.
An SME Growth Fund of ₹10,000 crore was announced for Champion SMEs.
The ECMS outlay was raised to ₹40,000 crore and Semiconductor Mission 2.0 announced.
₹20,000 crore over five years was allotted for carbon capture, utilisation and storage.
Rare Earth Corridors are planned in Odisha, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
A High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat was announced.
A Surat–Dankuni freight corridor, 7 high-speed rail corridors and 20 national waterways were announced.
Budget 2024-25 (23 July 2024): expenditure ₹48.21 lakh crore and fiscal deficit 4.9% of GDP.
Budget 2024-25 capex was ₹11.11 lakh crore (3.4% of GDP).
Budget 2024-25 raised the standard deduction to ₹75,000 and abolished angel tax.
FRBM Rules were notified in July 2004; guarantees are capped at 0.5% of GDP a year.
The 2018 FRBM amendment set FD 3% by 31 March 2021 and general government debt 60% (Centre 40%) by 2024-25.
FRBM requires a Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement, a Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement and a Macro-economic Framework Statement.
The 12th Finance Commission (C. Rangarajan, 2004) linked State debt relief to State fiscal responsibility laws.
N.K. Singh Committee: general government debt 60% of GDP — Centre 40%, States 20% — by 2023 (UPSC 2018).
N.K. Singh Committee FD path: 3% till 2020, 2.8% in 2020-21, 2.5% by 2023.
In 2008-09 the Centre's FD rose to 6.2% against 2.7% budgeted; States' limits were relaxed to 3.5% and 4%.
In 2019-20 the corporate tax cut was treated as a structural reform; FD was revised to 3.8% from 3.3%.
COVID-19 was treated as a national calamity invoking the escape clause.
The 16th FC wants the Centre's FD at 3.5% of GDP by 2030-31 and an end to off-budget borrowings.
The 16th FC projects combined debt falling from 77.3% to 73.1% of GDP by 2030-31.
Budget deficit = total expenditure − total receipts including borrowings; no longer used.
Crowding out: heavy government borrowing raises interest rates and squeezes private investment.
Deficit financing in India was used mainly for economic development (UPSC 2013).
Creating new money to finance a budget deficit is the most inflationary method (UPSC 2011).
To cut a persistent deficit: reduce revenue expenditure and rationalise subsidies (UPSC 2016).
With revenue expenditure 80,000, revenue receipts 60,000, borrowings 10,000 and interest 6,000 (₹ crore): RD 20,000, FD 10,000, PD 4,000 (UPSC 2025).
Gross primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest; FD 50,000 and interest 1,500 give 48,500 (UPSC 2025).
Impact is on the first payer; incidence is on whoever finally bears the tax.
Broadening the tax base raises revenue without raising rates.
Proportional = same rate; progressive = rate rises; regressive = rate falls; digressive = rises then constant.
Ad valorem tax is a percentage of value (GST); specific tax is a fixed amount per unit (excise on petrol).
MODVAT (1986) followed the L.K. Jha Committee's recommendation.
The Raja Chelliah Committee (1991-93) recommended broadening the base and simpler rates.
The Kelkar Committee (2002) proposed abolishing wealth tax; the Kelkar Task Force (2003-04) dealt with FRBM and first proposed GST.
MAT applies to zero-tax companies (present form 1997-98); AMT applies to non-corporate entities.
The September 2019 corporate tax cut set 22% for existing and 15% for new manufacturing companies.
Capital gains are long-term after 36 months (source text); since July 2024 listed securities need 12 months.
Securities Transaction Tax was introduced in 2004.
Banking Cash Transaction Tax ran from 2005 to 2009.
The 6% equalisation levy (Google tax) on online ads (2016) was abolished from 1 April 2025.
Professional tax is levied by States under Article 276, capped at ₹2,500 a year.
New-regime slabs: nil to 4 lakh, 5% to 8, 10% to 12, 15% to 16, 20% to 20, 25% to 24, 30% above.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the Income Tax Act, 1961 from 1 April 2026.
The Income-tax Bill 2025 was examined by a Select Committee chaired by Baijayant Panda.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 has about 536 sections and replaces previous/assessment year with a single tax year.
The Direct Taxes Code Bill, 2010 sought to replace the Income Tax Act 1961 and Wealth Tax Act 1957.
Customs duty is levied under the Customs Act, 1962.
Countervailing duty offsets a foreign export subsidy; anti-dumping duty targets below-cost imports; both on DGTR advice.
Sales tax on toothpaste was imposed and collected by the State Government (UPSC 2014).
Service tax began in 1994 and was subsumed in GST on 1 July 2017.
Stamp duty is a State tax on property documents.
VAT avoids the cascading effect through Input Tax Credit.
VAT was a State subject, introduced by States from 1 April 2005 (UPSC 2011).
GAAR came into effect on 1 April 2017.
DTAAs avoid double taxation by the exemption or credit method; India has 90+ such treaties.
Place of Effective Management decides a company's tax residence (from 2017).
BEPS is an OECD initiative (2013) to curb tax avoidance by multinational companies (UPSC 2016).
The OECD/G20 global minimum corporate tax is 15% under Pillar Two.
Hawala is illegal under FEMA and PMLA.
Tax avoidance is legal use of loopholes; tax evasion is illegal concealment.
A tax shelter is legal and domestic; a tax haven is a low-tax jurisdiction abroad such as the Cayman Islands or Mauritius.
The Tobin tax (James Tobin) is also called the Financial Transaction Tax or Robin Hood tax.
Presumptive tax estimates income as a fixed share of a small business's turnover.
A robot tax is a proposed levy on automation that displaces workers.
The 122nd Amendment Bill (2014) became the 101st Amendment Act; Assam was the first State to ratify.
Article 246A gives power to make GST laws, 269A provides IGST and 279A the GST Council.
1 July is observed as GST Day.
The Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers on GST was chaired by Asim Dasgupta.
The Arvind Subramanian Committee (2015) suggested a revenue-neutral GST rate of 15-15.5%.
GST Council members include the MoS Revenue and State FMs including Delhi and Puducherry; States elect a Vice-Chairperson.
Alcohol for human consumption is constitutionally outside GST; five petroleum products await a Council-recommended date.
Lottery, betting and gambling are taxable under GST.
Cereal grains hulled, cooked chicken eggs and newspapers are GST-exempt; processed canned fish is taxed (UPSC 2018).
GST's advantage is a single common market replacing multiple taxes, not cutting CAD (UPSC 2017).
GST compensation to States ran for 5 years (to June 2022) assuming 14% annual revenue growth.
The GST composition scheme is for turnover up to ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh in NE States and HP) with no input tax credit.
NAPA under the CGST Act checked profiteering; its work moved to the CCI in December 2022 and anti-profiteering ended from 1 April 2025.
GSTN is a non-profit IT backbone 100% owned by the Centre and States.
An e-way bill is needed for goods above ₹50,000 moved more than 10 km.
GSTAT is the GST Appellate Tribunal for GST disputes, principal bench New Delhi.
GST 2.0 was approved by the 56th GST Council meeting on 3 September 2025 after the PM's 15 August 2025 announcement.
State GST is AP's largest own-tax source (36% in 2026-27).
The FC (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951 provides a Chairman and four members.
The divisible pool excludes cesses, surcharges and cost of collection.
Vertical devolution is States' share of the pool; horizontal devolution is its split among States.
Article 270 shares central taxes; Article 275 gives statutory grants; Article 282 discretionary grants.
The 1st Finance Commission was chaired by K.C. Neogy.
The 13th FC was chaired by Vijay Kelkar and the 15th by N.K. Singh.
The 15th FC's 41% was 1% less than 42% because J&K became a UT; it introduced demographic performance.
16th FC members: Ajay Narayan Jha, Annie George Mathew, Manoj Panda; Soumya Kanti Ghosh part-time; Ritvik Pandey Secretary.
The 16th FC report was tabled on 1 February 2026 and kept the States' share at 41%.
The 16th FC gives income distance 42.5% and population 17.5% weight.
The 16th FC added a new criterion, contribution to GDP (10%), replacing tax and fiscal effort.
The 16th FC kept forest at 10% but counts open forest and increase in forest cover 2015-23.
The 16th FC redefined demographic performance as population growth 1971-2011 (weight 10%).
The 16th FC recommended ₹9.47 lakh crore of grants and discontinued revenue-deficit, sector-specific and State-specific grants.
Local body grants are 80% basic and 20% performance; rural ₹4.35 lakh crore, urban ₹3.56 lakh crore.
Disaster fund cost sharing is 90:10 for NE and Himalayan States and 75:25 for others.
Special infrastructure grants (₹56,100 crore) fund wastewater systems in cities of 10-40 lakh.
The 16th FC asked States to close 308 inactive State PSUs and privatise DISCOMs.
AP's share in central taxes: 4.31% (14th FC), 4.05% (15th), 4.22% (16th).
AP's 16th FC grants: rural local bodies ₹16,627 crore, urban ₹12,158 crore, disaster ₹6,125 crore.
Visakhapatnam and Vijayawada are eligible for 16th FC special infrastructure grants (up to ₹5,000 crore each).
AP's per-capita social-security pension spending is ₹5,061; a check found 9% of beneficiaries ineligible.
AP Budget 2026-27 was presented by Payyavula Keshav on 14 February 2026.
AP revenue receipts 2026-27: ₹2,34,140 crore — 59% own resources, 41% from the Centre.
AP's share in central taxes is ₹64,362 crore and central grants ₹32,458 crore in 2026-27.
AP projects stamp duty and registration fees to rise 70% in 2026-27.
AP capital outlay 2026-27 is ₹48,698 crore, up 47%.
AP revenue expenditure 2026-27 is ₹2,56,143 crore.
AP will spend ₹37,281 crore on interest (16% of revenue receipts) and ₹23,713 crore on pensions.
AP's 2025-26 revised fiscal deficit is 4.6% of GSDP (budgeted 4.4%); revised revenue deficit 2.3%.
AP outstanding liabilities are 36% of GSDP (33% in 2021-22).
AP outstanding guarantees were ₹1,77,328 crore (10% of GSDP) in December 2025.
CAG (2024) put AP's off-budget borrowings at ₹1.28 lakh crore (9.7% of GSDP) in March 2023.
Central 50-year interest-free capex loans (AP ₹11,000 crore) are excluded from the borrowing ceiling.
AP real GSDP grew 8% in 2024-25 against India's 6.5%.
AP 2024-25 sector shares: agriculture 37%, industry 21%, services 42%.
AP per-capita GSDP was ₹2,98,058 in 2024-25 vs India ₹2,34,859.
From 1 April 2026 AP gives handloom weavers 200 units and power-loom weavers 500 units of free power a month.
AP will set up the Andhra Pradesh Wealth Fund as a sovereign wealth fund.
Harita Andhra Pradesh targets green cover of 37% by 2030 and 50% by 2047.
NTR Bharosa pensions get ₹27,719 crore in 2026-27.
Stree Shakti (free bus travel for women) gets ₹1,420 crore; NTR Vaidya Seva ₹4,000 crore.
AP allots 11.7% of spending to education against a 14.5% State average; roads only 0.9%.
Only 16% of AP's auctioned mineral blocks were operational (January 2025); mining non-tax revenue ₹5,196 crore.
